How healthy we are across the lifespan, including how well we age, depends partly on conditions
before birth and in early postnatal life. That is the premise of the developmental origins of
health and disease (DOHaD). I study it through the gut, where maternal exposures, the first
colonizing microbes, and host development meet. The sections below follow that path in developmental order,
from how maternal diet programs the fetal gut, to when colonization begins, to how a mother's
pregnancy history shapes what she transmits.

## Maternal diet, the placenta, and the fetal gut

::: {.key-finding}
In mice, maternal high-fat diet disrupts the gut–placenta–fetus axis, and its effects on the
offspring gut persist into adulthood.
:::

My doctoral work used a mouse model of diet-induced obesity to trace how maternal diet affects the
gut–placenta–fetus axis. Characterizing the maternal gut microbiome, maternal intestine, placenta,
and fetal intestine in the same cohort revealed a chain running from diet to fetus: disrupted
maternal intestinal adaptation to pregnancy, placental hypoxia, and altered barrier protein and
immune marker profiles in the fetal gut. That chain is not visible in studies of a single
compartment.

Follow-up work showed that the fetal intestinal inflammation depends on TNF signalling, and that
the effects persist. In adulthood, offspring had altered gut microbiota composition, increased gut
barrier permeability, and greater susceptibility to a postnatal dietary challenge.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Gohir, Kennedy et al. 2019, *J Physiol*](https://doi.org/10.1113/JP277353) ·
PhD thesis, McMaster University, 2021
:::

## When does microbial colonization begin?

::: {.key-finding}
Meconium collected before birth has no detectable microbiota, so gut colonization begins at birth.
:::

For close to a decade, whether microbial colonization begins before birth was one of the most
contested questions in microbiome science. A substantial literature reported bacterial DNA in
placenta, amniotic fluid, and meconium, which would mean the fetal environment is not sterile and
that microbes shape development earlier than assumed.

Most of those studies lacked the contamination controls that low-biomass samples require. When a
sample contains very little microbial DNA, reagent- and laboratory-derived sequences can dominate
the result while still looking biologically plausible. Through a collaboration with
Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin, I applied contamination-aware protocols to meconium collected
immediately before caesarean delivery and found no detectable microbiota. That attention to
technical artefacts goes back to my MSc work, which showed that PCR amplification introduces
consistent, primer- and region-dependent biases in Illumina-based 16S rRNA gene profiling.

I then re-analysed the published data behind a high-profile paper that I thought overstated the
evidence for fetal microbial exposure, which became a peer-reviewed letter in *Cell*. The letter
led to my being first author on a *Nature* perspective, written with 47 colleagues, that
synthesized the evidence and set out principles for contamination-aware study design.

If the fetus is not colonized, any prenatal influence of the maternal microbiome has to operate
through bacterial products, such as metabolites or extracellular vesicles, that cross the
placenta. Which of these signals reach the fetus, and what they do to fetal development, is still
largely unknown.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Kennedy et al. 2021, *Nat Microbiol*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-021-00904-0) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2021, *Cell*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2021.10.026) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2023, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05546-8) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2014, *Appl Environ Microbiol*](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.01451-14)
:::

## Parity as a modifier

::: {.key-finding}
Parity modifies how maternal adiposity relates to the gut microbiota in pregnancy, and the
differences extend to neonatal colonization.
:::

Pregnancy microbiome studies generally treat consecutive pregnancies as interchangeable. Yet
first-born children are smaller at birth, one sign that first and later pregnancies differ
biologically.

In a prospective cohort at Charité, I found that parity modifies how BMI and gestational weight
gain relate to the maternal gut microbiota. Associations between excess adiposity and community
composition were largely confined to first pregnancies, and multiparous participants followed
different microbial trajectories. With McMaster's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, I
developed TALDA, which adapts latent Dirichlet allocation to model subcommunities of co-occurring
taxa over time; in this cohort, specific subcommunities expand and contract differently in first
and later pregnancies, and their postpartum recovery diverges. Pooling primiparous and multiparous participants can therefore
obscure real biological signal. In neonates, delivery mode, birth order, and sex each
independently shape early colonization.

In the Baby & Mi birth cohort, I am now asking how intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and birth
order jointly shape infant microbiome development, and whether early disruptions propagate to
later growth and atopic outcomes.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Kennedy et al. 2023, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2023.2259316) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2025, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2025.2491667) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2026, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2026.2690907)
:::

## From early life to healthspan

The question that runs through all of this work is which early-life differences last, and which
can be changed. The next step is to follow them forward, from childhood growth and allergy to gut
barrier function and health in aging, and to ask where along that path prevention could start.

Early-life programming is well established as a factor in who is susceptible to diet- and
lifestyle-related disease. Whether it also shapes who benefits from interventions, such as changes
in diet or exercise, is largely untested, and the answer could help match prevention to the people
most likely to benefit. Closer to birth, the Good Bugs Study, which I lead, asks which members of
the vaginal microbiota protect mothers and newborns against Group B *Streptococcus*.
